nameStory: The 'tick-trefoil' name comes from this plant's sneaky seed pods that stick to your clothes and socks just like ticks! The seeds have tiny hooked hairs that grab onto fabric and fur, earning them the nickname 'beggar's lice.' The 'trefoil' part refers to the three-part leaves, though this species is called 'toothed' because its leaflets have pointed, serrated edges.
description: Toothed tick-trefoil is a slender, upright wildflower that grows 2-4 feet tall in New England's woodlands and forest edges. This member of the legume family produces small pink to purple pea-like flowers in late summer, followed by flat, segmented seed pods that readily stick to passing animals and hikers. The plant has the characteristic three-leaflet structure of many legumes, but its leaflets are distinctly pointed and toothed along the edges. It's a native wildflower that plays an important role in forest ecosystems, fixing nitrogen in the soil while providing food for wildlife.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-part leaves with distinctly pointed, tooth-edged leaflets that feel slightly rough to the touch and are arranged alternately along the stem

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink to purple pea-like flowers clustered in loose, branching sprays that appear in late summer, each flower about 1/4 inch long

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, segmented seed pods that break apart into triangular sections covered with tiny hooked hairs that stick firmly to clothing and fur

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright, somewhat branching stem reaching 2-4 feet tall with a slender, graceful appearance and sparse foliage

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Smooth to slightly hairy green stems that feel firm but flexible when gently bent

habitat: Look for toothed tick-trefoil in partially shaded woodlands, forest edges, and clearings throughout New England. It prefers well-drained soils and is often found along woodland trails, in gaps between trees, and at the borders where forests meet fields. You'll typically find it growing alongside other woodland wildflowers and shrubs in areas that get dappled sunlight.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as the forest canopy leafs out, with fresh three-part leaves appearing on slender stems.
seasonality.summer: The plant reaches full height and produces its characteristic pink to purple flowers in loose clusters from mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Flowers give way to the notorious sticky seed pods that cling to everything, while leaves may turn yellowish before dropping.
seasonality.winter: The plant dies back completely, leaving only the root system underground to regenerate next spring.

funFact: Toothed tick-trefoil's sticky seeds are so effective at hitchhiking that they inspired part of the invention of Velcro! The tiny hooked hairs on the seed pods grab onto fabric fibers the same way Velcro hooks catch onto loops, making this humble woodland plant a contributor to modern fastening technology.
confusionNotes: With 10 different tick-trefoil species in New England, identification can be tricky! The key is in the leaves - toothed tick-trefoil has distinctly pointed, serrated leaflets, while most others have smoother or more rounded leaf edges. Remember: 'toothed' means the leaves have teeth (serrations) along their edges.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name containing 'tick,' this plant is completely harmless and unrelated to actual ticks. The name refers only to how the seeds stick to you, not to any disease-carrying insects. Many people call the seeds 'beggar's lice' or 'sticktights' due to their persistent clinging ability.
compareHints: Among its tick-trefoil relatives, the toothed variety stands out for its distinctly serrated leaf edges - most other species have smooth or only slightly toothed leaflets. Showy tick-trefoil is much taller with showier flower clusters, while trailing tick-trefoil has round leaves and creeps along the ground. The pointed, clearly toothed leaflets are your best clue for proper identification.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its tick-trefoil relatives, showy tick-trefoil is typically the tallest and most robust, with the largest and most densely packed flower clusters.

Among New England's many ticktrefoils, panicled ticktrefoil stands out with its distinctly narrow, lance-shaped leaflets - much thinner than the broad leaflets of showy tick-trefoil or the rounded leaves of round-leaved trailing tick-trefoil.
Among the tick-trefoils, this is the only one with perfectly round leaflets and a distinctly trailing growth habit.
Among the tick-trefoils, this species stands out for its height and smooth appearance.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, Maryland tick-trefoil is distinguished by its relatively small, smooth leaflets and delicate overall appearance.
Among its tick-trefoil relatives, little-leaf stands out for its distinctly smaller leaflets and notably hairy stems.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, perplexed tick-trefoil is most easily confused with tall tick-trefoil, requiring expert examination to separate reliably.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, hoary tick-trefoil is the gray ghost - its fuzzy, grayish appearance makes it unmistakable.
Among New England's ticktrefoils, sessileleaf is the only one with leaves that attach directly to the stem without stalks - all its relatives have obvious leaf stems.
Among the tick-trefoils, stiff tick-trefoil stands out for its rigid, unbending stems - most others like showy tick-trefoil or panicled tick-trefoil have flexible stems that sway easily.
